summary: Apomorphine is a potent non-ergot dopamine agonist for the acute, intermittent treatment of hypomobility ('off' episodes) in advanced Parkinson disease. Apokyn is given by SUBCUTANEOUS injection (never IV) and Kynmobi is a sublingual film. It causes SEVERE NAUSEA and vomiting, so patients must be PRETREATED with the antiemetic trimethobenzamide; 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron, alosetron) are CONTRAINDICATED because profound hypotension and loss of consciousness have occurred when combined. A supervised test dose with supine and standing blood pressure monitoring is mandatory. Major risks include orthostatic/profound hypotension, syncope, somnolence and sudden sleep attacks, hallucinations, dyskinesia, QT prolongation, impulse control disorders and priapism.
indications: Acute, intermittent treatment of hypomobility, 'off' episodes ('end-of-dose wearing off' and unpredictable 'on/off' episodes) associated with advanced Parkinson disease

dosage.d: 0.2 mL (2 mg) SC during an 'off' period with supine and standing BP measured pre-dose and at 20, 40 and 60 min
dosage.n: If tolerated and responsive, start at 0.2 mL (2 mg); if hypotensive, do not initiate

dosage.d: 0.2 mL (2 mg) SC per 'off' episode after a tolerated 2 mg test dose
dosage.n: Begin pretreatment with trimethobenzamide 300 mg PO TID 3 days before initiation

dosage.d: Increase by 0.1 mL (1 mg) every few days as tolerated; usual effective dose 0.2-0.6 mL (2-6 mg) per 'off' episode
dosage.n: Do not increase faster than recommended; max single dose 0.6 mL (6 mg)

dosage.d: Up to 5 doses/day; do not exceed total 20 mg/day; allow >=2 h between doses
dosage.n: Average 3 doses/day in trials; re-administration for a single 'off' episode not studied

dosage.d: Restart at 0.2 mL (2 mg) test dose and re-titrate
dosage.n: Loss of tolerance to hypotensive effects may occur with interruption

admin: Give by SUBCUTANEOUS injection ONLY - NEVER intravenously (IV use has caused thrombus formation, pulmonary embolism and serious morbidity)
PRETREAT with the antiemetic trimethobenzamide 300 mg orally three times daily, starting 3 days before the first dose, and continue for at least the first 2 months
Perform an initial test dose under medical supervision with supine and standing blood pressure monitoring
Rotate injection sites; doses are measured in mL of the 10 mg/mL solution using the multiple-dose pen
Do NOT use 5-HT3 antiemetics (ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron, alosetron) - combination is contraindicated
Kynmobi sublingual film: place under the tongue and allow to dissolve completely; do not chew or swallow
moa: Apomorphine is a non-ergoline dopamine agonist that stimulates postsynaptic dopamine D2-type receptors within the caudate-putamen of the brain, mimicking dopamine and improving motor function during 'off' periods in Parkinson disease. Its benefit in hypomobility is believed to result from this D2 receptor agonism rather than any opioid activity (it is not an opioid despite the name).

absolute: Concomitant use of 5-HT3 antagonist antiemetics (ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron) or alosetron - profound hypotension and loss of consciousness reported
Known hypersensitivity to apomorphine or any product ingredient (including sodium metabisulfite/sulfites)
relative: Significant orthostatic hypotension or cardiovascular/cerebrovascular disease
Known QT prolongation or use of QT-prolonging drugs
History of somnolence/sleep attacks while driving
History of impulse control disorders or psychosis
monitor: Supine and standing blood pressure with each titration step
Daytime somnolence and episodes of falling asleep
QTc in patients at risk, and mental status for hallucinations/psychosis

preg: Limited human data. Apomorphine produced adverse developmental effects in animals at clinically relevant doses. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: There are no data on the presence of apomorphine in human milk, its effects on the breastfed infant, or on milk production. Consider the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding along with the mother's clinical need and any potential adverse effects on the infant.
renal: Apomorphine plasma concentrations are increased in renal impairment. Reduce the test dose and starting dose and use with caution; titrate carefully while monitoring blood pressure.
hepatic: Use with caution; exposure may be increased. Avoid in moderate to severe hepatic impairment. Monitor for enhanced hypotensive and adverse CNS effects.

major: 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron) and alosetron - CONTRAINDICATED; profound hypotension and loss of consciousness
Antihypertensives and vasodilators - additive hypotension and risk of serious falls/syncope
QT-prolonging drugs (class IA/III antiarrhythmics, certain antipsychotics) - additive risk of torsades de pointes
moderate: Dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) - may reduce apomorphine efficacy
CNS depressants and sedatives - additive somnolence/sleep attacks
Other dopaminergic Parkinson therapies - additive dyskinesia and impulse control effects
minor: Drugs affecting sulfite sensitivity in susceptible patients (product contains sodium metabisulfite)
interactions.food: Subcutaneous administration is not affected by food; the sublingual film may be taken without regard to meals. Avoid grapefruit only if combined QT-prolonging agents apply.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive hypotension and central nervous system depression increase the risk of syncope, somnolence and falls.
interactions.diagnostics: May prolong the QT interval on ECG; can lower blood pressure on orthostatic testing.

common: Nausea and vomiting (severe - requires antiemetic pretreatment)
serious: Sudden onset of sleep / sleep attacks during activities including driving
Impulse control disorders (gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive spending/eating)
QT prolongation and risk of torsades de pointes
rare: Withdrawal-emergent hyperpyrexia and confusion on abrupt discontinuation
emergency: Loss of consciousness / profound hypotension (especially if a 5-HT3 antagonist was given)
Pulmonary embolism or thrombus formation after inadvertent IV administration
Sustained painful priapism requiring urological care

monitoring: Supine and standing blood pressure at the test dose and at each titration step
Daytime somnolence and any episodes of falling asleep during activities
Mental status for hallucinations, confusion and psychotic behavior
Behavior for new or worsening impulse control disorders
ECG/QTc in patients with cardiac risk or on QT-prolonging drugs
counsel: You must take your antiemetic (trimethobenzamide) starting 3 days before and during early treatment - do NOT use ondansetron or similar drugs
This medicine is injected under the skin (or dissolved under the tongue) - it must NEVER be given into a vein
Stand up slowly; the drug can cause severe drops in blood pressure, dizziness and fainting
Do not drive or operate machinery if you experience drowsiness or sudden sleep attacks
Tell your doctor about new urges to gamble, shop, eat or increased sexual urges
Seek urgent care for a prolonged or painful erection (priapism), or for severe vomiting, fainting or chest pain
Avoid alcohol and tell your doctor about all other medicines, including heart-rhythm and blood-pressure drugs
pk: Motor improvement within ~10-20 min of SC injection
Plasma Tmax ~10-60 min; clinical effect peaks ~10-20 min
Benefit lasts up to ~90 min per dose
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from freezing
pearls: SEVERE nausea/vomiting is expected - pretreat with trimethobenzamide and NEVER use a 5-HT3 antagonist (ondansetron etc.) which is contraindicated (profound hypotension, loss of consciousness)
NEVER give IV - intravenous administration has caused thrombus formation and pulmonary embolism
Always do a supervised test dose with supine and standing blood pressure before starting
Doses are written in mL of the 10 mg/mL solution; do not increase faster than recommended
It is a dopamine agonist, NOT an opioid, despite the 'morphine' in its name - naloxone is not the treatment
Watch for impulse control disorders, sudden sleep attacks, hallucinations, QT prolongation and priapism
missed: Apomorphine is used as needed for acute 'off' episodes, so there is no fixed dose schedule to miss. Use a dose only when an 'off' episode occurs, allow at least 2 hours between doses, and do not exceed 5 doses or 20 mg per day. If treatment has been interrupted for more than one week, contact the prescriber to restart with a supervised 2 mg test dose.
overdose: Overdose may cause severe hypotension, profound vomiting, bradycardia, sedation, respiratory depression and CNS stimulation. There is no specific antidote. Treat supportively: place the patient supine with legs elevated, give IV fluids and vasopressors for hypotension, and monitor cardiac rhythm. Because it is NOT an opioid, naloxone is not expected to reverse it. Note that domperidone or other non-5-HT3 measures, not 5-HT3 antagonists, should be used for vomiting.
